summary: This is the rolling-direction (RD) tensile specimen of a low-density Fe-7.95Mn-0.25C-4.94Al (wt.%) medium-Mn lightweight steel after intercritical annealing at 850 °C for 10 min and water quenching. Loaded in uniaxial tension parallel to the banding direction, it was used to resolve why the banded δ-ferrite + ultrafine-grained (UFG) γ+α microstructure exhibits anisotropic strain hardening and strain-induced martensite (TRIP) kinetics relative to the transverse direction.
composition: The nominal composition is Fe-7.95Mn-0.25C-4.94Al (wt.%), with Fe as the matrix element. Mn and C stabilize austenite, while the high Al addition (~4.94 wt.%) reduces the mass density to ~7.40 g/cm³ (a 6.2% reduction attributed to the Al content) and promotes δ-ferrite formation; the Thermo-Calc pseudo-binary phase diagram shows that at 850 °C this alloy lies within the γ+α two-phase field.
processing: Ingots were prepared by vacuum induction melting and then homogenized at 1100 °C. They were hot-rolled at temperatures maintained above ~1000 °C to a thickness of ~3 mm, followed by cold rolling to a final thickness of ~1.5 mm. The cold-rolled sheet was intercritically annealed at 850 °C for 10 minutes and water-quenched to room temperature, intended to produce the ultrafine γ+α aggregate plus δ-ferrite. For this sample, subsequent uniaxial tensile testing was performed at room temperature with the loading axis along the rolling direction, i.e. parallel to the banding direction.
microstructure: The non-deformed microstructure is a banded/layered composite aligned along RD, composed of coarse-grained δ-ferrite (BCC, ~44 vol.%, average grain size ~38 μm, {100}<011> rotated-cube texture with <011>//RD and {100}//ND and a maximum intensity of 2.57) and an ultrafine-grained γ+α aggregate (~56 vol.%) that reversely transformed from martensite during annealing. Within this aggregate, austenite (FCC, ~38.8 vol.% by EBSD, ~1.8 μm) and α-ferrite (BCC, ~25 vol.%, ~2 μm) are both ultrafine. The δ-ferrite was retained from hot rolling and underwent rapid recrystallization and grain growth during intercritical annealing. The uniform BCC image quality in the undeformed state confirms the absence of martensite before deformation.
properties: Tested at room temperature under quasi-static uniaxial tension at ~1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (HEXRD gauge length 12 mm, width 2 mm, thickness 1.2 mm; μ-DIC dog-bone gauge length 20 mm), the RD specimen reached an ultimate tensile strength of 864 MPa and a total elongation of 69%, higher than the TD orientation, with a maximum strain-hardening rate of 2052 MPa. Local Vickers hardness was 221 ± 3.0 HV in the UFG γ+α region versus 205 ± 1.5 HV in δ-ferrite. The calculated mass density is ~7.40 g/cm³. Characterization combined EBSD (Zeiss-Crossbeam 340 SEM; TSL OIM and AZtecCrystal), TEM (FEI Talos F200X at 200 kV), Vickers microhardness testing, in-situ synchrotron HEXRD (PETRA III P02.1, ~60 keV) and high-resolution μ-DIC with nano-scale gold speckles.
mechanisms: Austenite is intrinsically softer than ferrite in this steel: its weighted-average lattice strain deviates from linearity at 1.8% applied strain in the RD sample, versus 2.3% for ferrite, so plastic strain localizes preferentially within austenite in the ultrafine-grained γ+α aggregate.

When the banded microstructure is loaded along RD (bands parallel to the loading axis), the coarse δ-ferrite and the UFG γ+α aggregate deform at similar strain levels under an iso-strain condition, as confirmed by μ-DIC strain profiles and statistical averages.

To maintain iso-strain compatibility between the harder UFG γ+α region (221 ± 3.0 HV) and the softer δ-ferrite (205 ± 1.5 HV), a high density of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) accumulates at the δ-ferrite/UFG γ+α phase boundary, providing additional martensite nucleation sites and a larger local driving force.

Strain-induced α'-martensite nucleates preferentially at austenite/ferrite (α or δ) phase boundaries, because the stress/strain concentrations and interfacial defects (e.g. ledges) there promote shear-band intersections, as shown by EBSD KAM and TEM.

The higher local austenite strain in the RD sample (about 1.15× that of TD, per μ-DIC) accelerates strain-induced α'-martensite formation (TRIP effect), which raises the strain-hardening rate to a maximum of 2052 MPa and produces higher strength and ductility.

Austenite deforms by planar dislocation slip with dense stacking faults owing to its low stacking-fault energy, whereas α- and δ-ferrite deform by dislocation cross-slip and tangle formation at higher stacking-fault energy.

The loading-direction dependence of martensite kinetics is reproduced by the Olson-Cohen model using ε_RD = 1.15 ε_TD for the austenite plastic strain, confirming that strain partitioning—rather than the weak δ-ferrite texture (maximum intensity 2.57) or the nearly equal Taylor factors—controls the transformation kinetics.
conclusions: The RD sample's superior strength (864 MPa) and ductility (69%) relative to TD arise from its higher strain-hardening capability, which is linked to faster strain-induced α'-martensite kinetics and a higher austenite dislocation density. Loading parallel to the banding direction places the δ-ferrite and UFG γ+α aggregate under an iso-strain condition with similar deformation levels, whereas TD loading induces an iso-stress-like response with strain concentrating in the softer δ-ferrite. This direction-dependent strain distribution—not the weak δ-ferrite texture or the nearly equal Taylor factors—governs the martensite transformation kinetics and hence the TRIP hardening. Such loading-direction anisotropy should be considered in alloy and microstructure design for improved formability under multi-axial loading.
unmapped: Olson–Cohen model fitting for the transformation kinetics used parameters α = 1.35, β = 2 and n = 2, with an initial austenite fraction F_γ0 = 46.5 vol.%; the model reproduced the RD kinetics when the austenite plastic strain was set to ε_RD = 1.15 ε_TD, although it slightly under-predicted the martensite fraction at high strain.
